abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a fundamental paradigm for expanding Large Language Models beyond their static training limitations. However, a critical misalignment exists between current RAG capabilities and real-world information environments. Modern knowledge repositories are inherently multimodal, containing rich combinations of textual content, visual elements, structured tables, and mathematical expressions. Yet existing RAG frameworks are limited to textual content, creating fundamental gaps when processing multimodal documents. We present RAG-Anything, a unified framework that enables comprehensive knowledge retrieval across all modalities. Our approach reconceptualizes multimodal content as interconnected knowledge entities rather than isolated data types. The framework introduces dual-graph construction to capture both cross-modal relationships and textual semantics within a unified representation. We develop cross-modal hybrid retrieval that combines structural knowledge navigation with semantic matching. This enables effective reasoning over heterogeneous content where relevant evidence spans multiple modalities. RAG-Anything demonstrates superior performance on challenging multimodal benchmarks, achieving significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. Performance gains become particularly pronounced on long documents where traditional approaches fail. Our framework establishes a new paradigm for multimodal knowledge access, eliminating the architectural fragmentation that constrains current systems. Our framework is open-sourced at: https://github.com/HKUDS/RAG-Anything.

sections.body: The introduction argues that existing RAG frameworks focus exclusively on text-only knowledge, while real-world documents combine text, visual elements, structured tables, and mathematical expressions. It names three challenges: unified multimodal representation, structure-aware decomposition, and cross-modal retrieval. The proposed framework uses a dual-graph construction and a cross-modal hybrid retrieval mechanism. The authors report experiments on DocBench and MMLongBench and state that gains increase with content length, and that graph-based representation provides the primary performance gains.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing RAG systems handle only text, so multimodal documents are poorly served; the paper proposes RAG-Anything to fix this.

sections.body: The method decomposes each source into atomic units with a modality type and raw content. A cross-modal knowledge graph anchors non-text units with multimodal entity nodes and `belongs_to` edges. A text-based graph is built with LightRAG-style extraction, and the two graphs are merged by entity alignment on entity names. Retrieval combines structural neighborhood expansion with dense similarity search over an embedding table, then fuses candidates with multi-signal scoring. The answer is produced by a vision-language model conditioned on the query, textual context, and recovered visual content.
sections.heading: The RAG-Anything Framework
sections.headline: RAG-Anything decomposes documents into typed units, builds two linked graphs, and retrieves through both structure and embeddings.

sections.body: The evaluation uses DocBench (229 documents, 1,102 questions) and MMLongBench (135 documents, 1,082 questions), with GPT-4o-mini as the backbone and accuracy judged by GPT-4o-mini. On DocBench, RAG-Anything reaches 63.4% overall against 61.0% for MMGraphRAG and 58.4% for LightRAG. The text reports a gap of over 13 points for documents exceeding 100 pages. An ablation on DocBench gives 60.0% for chunk-only retrieval and 62.4% without the reranker, against 63.4% for the full model. The text attributes most of the gain to graph-based retrieval rather than reranking.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: On MMLongBench, RAG-Anything scores 42.8% overall versus 37.7% for MMGraphRAG, with gains growing on longer documents.

sections.body: The related-work section reviews graph-enhanced RAG, including GraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG, and RAPTOR, and notes that these systems are text-centric. It then reviews multimodal RAG methods such as VideoRAG, MM-VID, VisRAG, and MMGraphRAG. The authors state that these approaches rely on modality-specific architectures, which they describe as architectural fragmentation. They position RAG-Anything as a unified graph-based framework that processes all modalities with consistent structured modeling.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work groups graph-enhanced RAG and multimodal RAG, and argues that prior multimodal systems fragment by modality.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes the dual-graph construction and hybrid retrieval as the core contribution, and reports superior performance on long-context documents, particularly those exceeding 100 pages. It cites failure-case analysis in Appendix A.5. The two failure modes identified are text-centric retrieval bias, where systems prefer textual sources even when queries require visual information, and rigid spatial processing that does not adapt to non-standard layouts. The authors say these findings motivate adaptive spatial reasoning and layout-aware parsing.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The paper concludes that dual-graph retrieval helps long documents and identifies text-centric bias and rigid spatial processing as failure modes.

sections.body: The appendix gives per-category document and question counts and average page counts for DocBench (Table 5) and MMLongBench (Table 6). It adds two additional cases: a chart interpretation case and a tabular case where the highest AUPRC value is 0.506. It documents vision, table, and equation analysis prompts, and the accuracy evaluation prompt used with GPT-4o-mini. It closes with two failure cases, cross-modal misalignment and structural noise in an ambiguous table, where all evaluated methods gave incorrect answers.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, extra case studies, the three multimodal prompts, the accuracy prompt, and failure-case analyses.
